On the English coast stand giant concrete dishes, staring out to sea. They look like alien satellite dishes. But they were built to listen. For enemy planes!

Back in the 1920s, Britain was worried about bombers coming across the Channel, and radar didn't exist yet. So a scientist named William Tucker had an idea. If you can't see the planes coming, hear them!
It sounds ridiculous, right? Listening for planes with a wall? But they kept building them bigger. A twenty-foot dish. A thirty-foot dish. And then a giant curved wall, two hundred feet long!

You see, the curved concrete works like cupping your hand behind your ear. It gathers faint sound and focuses it onto one spot, where a microphone sat. A listener could hear engines over the sea long before anyone could see them. In tests, that meant several extra minutes of warning.
But planes kept getting faster, and the warning kept getting shorter. Then radar arrived, and the ears went silent. Yet they're still standing at Dungeness today, listening to nothing at all.
